body: The library has six study rooms on the first floor. Rooms 1–4 seat up to four people and Rooms 5 and 6 seat up to ten. All rooms have a whiteboard and a power socket; Rooms 5 and 6 also have a screen you can connect a laptop to.
## Booking

Rooms can be booked online or at the information desk up to seven days in advance. A booking lasts a maximum of two hours; if the room is still free at the end of your booking, you may extend it once by asking at the desk. Bookings not claimed within fifteen minutes of the start time are cancelled and the room is released to other users.
## Who can book
Any library member aged 16 or over. A member may make one booking per day. Groups should book under one name only.
## Rules

Food is not allowed in the study rooms, though drinks with lids are permitted. Please keep noise low: the rooms are not soundproof. Leave the room as you found it and rub the whiteboard clean. The library is not responsible for belongings left in rooms.
## Cancellations
If you no longer need a room, please cancel online or by phone so that someone else can use it. Members who fail to turn up three times in a month will lose the right to book for the following month.
texts.label: A
texts.title: Hillview Public Library — Using the study rooms

body: ## Term dates
Classes run for ten weeks from Monday 22 September to Friday 28 November, with no classes in the week beginning 27 October (half term).
## Fees

Most ten-week courses cost £120. Courses marked with an asterisk (*) use materials that must be paid for separately — pottery, for example, has a £30 materials fee. Fees are reduced by 50% for people receiving a state pension or unemployment benefit; proof is required at enrolment.
## Enrolment

Enrol online at any time, or in person at the main reception between 9 am and 7 pm on weekdays. Enrolment closes one week before the course starts. Courses with fewer than eight students two weeks before the start date will be cancelled and fees refunded in full.
## Refunds
If you withdraw before the first class, you receive a full refund minus a £10 administration charge. After the first class, no refund is given unless the college cancels the course.
## Parking and transport
The college car park is free after 5.30 pm, but spaces are limited. The number 14 bus stops directly outside the main entrance.
Please note that the college closes at 9.30 pm and all classes must finish by 9.15 pm to allow rooms to be cleared.

headings.text: Why desert sand cannot be used
Why the price of sand keeps rising
A resource used more than any other except water

paragraphs.text: Sand is everywhere, and yet almost nobody thinks about it. After water, it is the most used natural resource on Earth: around fifty billion tonnes are extracted every year, enough to build a wall twenty-seven metres high and twenty-seven metres wide around the equator. Concrete is roughly two-thirds sand, and so, in one form or another, are the glass in our windows, the asphalt on our roads and the silicon chips in our phones. Every new road, airport and apartment block begins with sand, and the world is currently building faster than at any time in its history. A single family house uses about two hundred tonnes of it, a hospital several thousand, and a kilometre of motorway tens of thousands. Demand has tripled in the past two decades, driven above all by the growth of cities in Asia and Africa.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: It might seem that a resource found in every desert could never run short. But desert sand is almost useless for construction. Blown by the wind for thousands of years, its grains have become smooth and round, and they do not lock together; concrete made from them simply crumbles. Builders need the rough, angular grains produced by rivers, lakes and the sea. This is why Dubai, a city surrounded by desert, imported sand from Australia to build some of its tallest towers, and why the price of usable sand has risen sharply in many countries over the past two decades. Sand dredged from the sea bed can be used, but it must first be washed to remove the salt, which would otherwise corrode the steel inside concrete. Good sand, in other words, is not something found lying about; it is a product that has to be located, cleaned and transported, and each of these steps has a cost.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Removing sand from rivers and coasts has consequences that are easy to overlook. When a river bed is dredged, the water flows faster and cuts deeper, undermining bridges and lowering the water table so that nearby wells run dry. Beaches from which sand has been taken retreat, and the coast behind them loses its natural protection against storms. In parts of South-East Asia entire islands have disappeared as their sand was shipped away to expand cities elsewhere. Because much of this extraction is unregulated, and in some regions is controlled by criminal groups, nobody knows exactly how much is taken each year. The people who suffer most are usually those living beside the rivers: fishermen whose catches decline as the water becomes cloudy, and villagers whose houses collapse into the widening channel. Where extraction is illegal, they have little chance of compensation.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Engineers are now searching for alternatives. Crushed rock can replace sand in concrete, though it takes more energy to produce. Recycled concrete from demolished buildings is another option, and in some countries construction waste already supplies a significant share of building material. Researchers have also developed a way of treating desert sand with a binding agent so that it can be pressed into bricks. The most effective measure, however, may be the simplest: designing buildings that use less concrete in the first place, and building fewer of them where they are not needed. Sand will not run out tomorrow, but the age of treating it as free is over. None of these alternatives is perfect: recycled concrete is weaker than new, and the treated desert bricks are so far suitable only for low buildings. Governments have begun to respond, with several countries now requiring a licence for every load taken from a river.
paragraphs.label: D

clips.context: A library announcement about new cards and rules.
clips.transcript: Attention, please, library members. This is a short announcement about changes from the first of June. Library cards issued before 2020 will stop working, so please bring your old card to the front desk and we'll give you a new one for free. You'll need to show something with your address on it, such as a bill. The new cards let you borrow up to fifteen items instead of ten, and loans now last three weeks rather than two. Fines for late books have been removed completely; instead, if a book is more than a month late, your card is blocked until it's returned. clips.context: A tutor discusses a student's field trip report on coastal erosion.
clips.transcript:
TUTOR: Come in, Mei. I've read the draft of your field trip report. Overall it's good, but let's talk about the section on erosion rates.
MEI: I was worried about that. The figures from the two beaches didn't match what I expected.
TUTOR: Which is fine — unexpected results are the interesting part. What I want you to avoid is explaining them away. You've written that the northern beach "must have been measured wrongly".
MEI: Well, it lost far less sand than the southern one, even though it's more exposed to the wind.
TUTOR: Think about what else differs. What's behind the northern beach?
MEI: The sea wall… and a line of dunes. Oh — the dunes. They'd absorb some of the wave energy.
TUTOR: That's a much better line to pursue. Now, the photographs. They're clear, but there's no scale in any of them.
MEI: I did put a ruler in some shots, but the file names got mixed up so I left them out.
TUTOR: Put them back in, even if you have to re-label them by hand. A reader can't judge the size of anything otherwise. Lastly, the conclusion is too long — it repeats the introduction almost word for word.
MEI: I thought I was supposed to summarise.
TUTOR: Summarise the findings, yes, but in three or four sentences. Cut it to half a page. And you don't need the section on tides at all — it's not relevant to your question.
MEI: OK. So: keep the erosion section but rethink the explanation, add the scaled photos, shorten the conclusion, remove tides. When do you need it?
TUTOR: The final version goes in on the twelfth, but send me the new draft by the fifth so I have time to look at it.

clips.context: A briefing for volunteers before a river clean-up.
clips.transcript: Thanks for coming, everyone. I'm Jo from the River Trust and I'll be running today's clean-up. A few things before we start. We'll be working along the stretch between the old mill and the footbridge — that's about two kilometres. Please don't go beyond the footbridge; the bank there is unstable. Everyone gets gloves, a litter picker and a bag. Put general rubbish in the black bags and anything that can be recycled — cans, plastic bottles, glass — in the clear ones. If you find anything sharp, like needles or broken glass, don't pick it up: mark the spot with one of the orange flags and tell me. The same goes for anything heavy, such as shopping trolleys or tyres; we'll come back for those with the van. We'll stop for a break at eleven at the mill car park, where there'll be hot drinks. The whole thing should finish by one. Oh, and we've got a competition: the team that collects the strangest object wins a voucher for the café. Last year it was a garden gnome. Let's go.

clips.context: Part of a lecture on the history of the pencil.
clips.transcript: This week's lecture is about an object so ordinary that we hardly notice it: the pencil. The story begins in the north of England in the sixteenth century, when a storm uprooted trees near the village of Borrowdale and exposed a deposit of a soft, black mineral. Local shepherds found it useful for marking their sheep. The material was assumed to be a form of lead, which is why we still talk about pencil "lead" today, although it contains no lead at all; it is graphite, a form of carbon. The Borrowdale deposit was remarkably pure, and for about two hundred years it was the only source of solid graphite in the world. The English government guarded the mine closely, and pieces of graphite were smuggled out and sold at high prices. The modern pencil, however, was not an English invention. In 1795 a French engineer, Nicolas-Jacques Conté, was asked to find a way of making pencils without English graphite, since France was at war with Britain. His solution was to grind low-quality graphite into powder, mix it with clay, and bake it. By changing the amount of clay, he could make the pencil harder or softer — and that is still the system used today. So the object we take for granted is the result of a storm, a shortage and a war.
